search_results.title: Measurement of the CKM angle $γ$ in $B^{\pm} \rightarrow D(\rightarrow K^{0}_{\rm S} h^{\prime+}h^{\prime-})h^{\pm}$ decays with a novel approach
search_results.snippet: A measurement of the CKM angle $γ$ and related strong-phase parameters is performed using a novel, model-independent approach in ${B^{\pm}\rightarrow D(\rightarrow K^{0}_{\rm S} h^{\prime+}h^{\prime-}) h^{\pm}}$ decays, where $h^{(\prime)} \equiv π, K$. The analysis uses a joint data sample of electron-positron collisions collected by the BESIII experiment at the Beijing Electron-Positron Collider II during 2010--2011 and 2021--2022, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 8 fb$^{-1}$, and proton-proton collisions collected by the LHCb experiment at the Large Hadron Collider during 2011--2018, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 9 fb$^{-1}$. The two datasets are analyzed simultaneously by applying per-event weights based on the amplitude variation over the $D$-decay phase space to enhance the sensitivity to $C\!P$-violating observables. The CKM angle $γ$ is determined to be $γ= (71.3\pm 5.0)^{\circ}$, which constitutes the most precise single measurement to date.

search_results.title: Search for High-energy Neutrinos from Binary Neutron Star Merger GW170817 with ANTARES, IceCube, and the Pierre Auger Observatory
search_results.snippet: The Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo observatories recently discovered gravitational waves from a binary neutron star inspiral. A short gamma-ray burst (GRB) that followed the merger of this binary was also recorded by the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (Fermi-GBM), and the Anticoincidence Shield for the Spectrometer for the International Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory (INTEGRAL), indicating particle acceleration by the source. The precise location of the event was determined by optical detections of emission following the merger. We searched for high-energy neutrinos from the merger in the GeV--EeV energy range using the ANTARES, IceCube, and Pierre Auger Observatories. No neutrinos directionally coincident with the source were detected within $\pm500$ s around the merger time. Additionally, no MeV neutrino burst signal was detected coincident with the merger. We further carried out an extended search in the direction of the source for high-energy neutrinos within the 14-day period following the merger, but found no evidence of emission. We used these results to probe dissipation mechanisms in relativistic outflows driven by the binary neutron star merger. The non-detection is consistent with model predictions of short GRBs observed at a large off-axis angle.

search_results.title: All-sky search for long-duration gravitational-wave transients in the first part of the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Observing run
search_results.snippet: We present an all-sky search for long-duration gravitational waves (GWs) from the first part of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA fourth observing run (O4), called O4a and comprising data taken between 24 May 2023 and 16 January 2024. The GW signals targeted by this search are the so-called "long-duration" (> 1 s) transients expected from a variety of astrophysical processes, including non-axisymmetric deformations in magnetars or eccentric binary coalescences. We make minimal assumptions on the emitted GW waveforms in terms of morphologies and durations. Overall, our search targets signals with durations ~1-1000 s and frequency content in the range 16-2048 Hz. In the absence of significant detections, we report the sensitivity limits of our search in terms of root-sum-square signal amplitude (hrss) of reference waveforms. These limits improve upon the results from the third LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observing run (O3) by about 30% on average. Moreover, this analysis demonstrates substantial progress in our ability to search for long-duration GW signals owing to enhancements in pipeline detection efficiencies. As detector sensitivities continue to advance and observational runs grow longer, unmodeled long-duration searches will increasingly be able to explore a range of compelling astrophysical scenarios involving neutron stars and black holes.

search_results.title: Observation of the rare $B^0_s\toμ^+μ^-$ decay from the combined analysis of CMS and LHCb data
search_results.snippet: A joint measurement is presented of the branching fractions $B^0_s\toμ^+μ^-$ and $B^0\toμ^+μ^-$ in proton-proton collisions at the LHC by the CMS and LHCb experiments. The data samples were collected in 2011 at a centre-of-mass energy of 7 TeV, and in 2012 at 8 TeV. The combined analysis produces the first observation of the $B^0_s\toμ^+μ^-$ decay, with a statistical significance exceeding six standard deviations, and the best measurement of its branching fraction so far. Furthermore, evidence for the $B^0\toμ^+μ^-$ decay is obtained with a statistical significance of three standard deviations. The branching fraction measurements are statistically compatible with SM predictions and impose stringent constraints on several theories beyond the SM.

search_results.title: All-sky Searches for Continuous Gravitational Waves from Isolated Neutron Stars in the Data from the First Part of the Fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Observing Run
search_results.snippet: We present results from an all-sky search for continuous gravitational waves, using three different methods applied to the first eight months of LIGO data from the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration s observing run. We aim at signals potentially emitted by rotating, non-axisymmetric isolated neutron star in the Milky Way. The analysis spans a frequency range from 20 Hz to 2000 Hz and accommodates frequency derivative magnitudes up to $10^{-8}$ Hz/s. No statistically significant periodic gravitational wave signals were detected. We establish 95% confidence-level (CL) frequentist upper limits on the dimensionless strain amplitudes. The most stringent population-averaged strain upper limits reach 9.7 $\times$ $10^{-26}$ near 290 Hz, matching the best previous constraints from 250 to $\sim$1700 Hz while extending coverage to a much broader spin-down range. At higher frequencies, the new limits improve upon previous results by factors of approximately $\sim$1.6. These constraints are applied to three astrophysical scenarios: 1) the distribution of galactic neutron stars as a function of spin frequency and ellipticity; 2) the contribution of millisecond pulsars to the GeV excess near the galactic center; and 3) the possible dark matter fraction composed of nearby inspiraling primordial binary black holes with asteroid-scale masses.

The analysis uses a joint data sample of electron-positron collisions collected by the BESIII experiment at the Beijing Electron-Positron Collider II during 2010--2011 and 2021--2022, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 8 fb$^{-1}$, and proton-proton collisions collected by the LHCb experiment at the Large Hadron Collider during 2011--2018, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 9 fb$^{-1}$. The two datasets are analyzed simultaneously by applying per-event weights based on the amplitude variation over the $D$-decay phase space to enhance the sensitivity to $C\!P$-violating observables. The CKM angle $γ$ is determined to be $γ= (71.3\pm 5.0)^{\circ}$, which constitutes the most precise single measurement to date.

evidence.title: Search for High-energy Neutrinos from Binary Neutron Star Merger GW170817 with ANTARES, IceCube, and the Pierre Auger Observatory
evidence.text: The Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo observatories recently discovered gravitational waves from a binary neutron star inspiral. A short gamma-ray burst (GRB) that followed the merger of this binary was also recorded by the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (Fermi-GBM), and the Anticoincidence Shield for the Spectrometer for the International Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory (INTEGRAL), indicating particle acceleration by the source. The precise location of the event was determined by optical detections of emission following the merger. We searched for high-energy neutrinos from the merger in the GeV--EeV energy range using the ANTARES, IceCube, and Pierre Auger Observatories. No neutrinos directionally coincident with the source were detected within $\pm500$ s around the merger time. Additionally, no MeV neutrino burst signal was detected coincident with the merger. We further carried out an extended search in the direction of the source for high-energy neutrinos within the 14-day period following the merger, but found no evidence of emission. We used these results to probe dissipation mechanisms in relativistic outflows driven by the binary neutron star merger. The non-detection is consistent with model predictions of short GRBs observed at a large off-axis angle.

evidence.title: All-sky search for long-duration gravitational-wave transients in the first part of the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Observing run
evidence.text: We present an all-sky search for long-duration gravitational waves (GWs) from the first part of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA fourth observing run (O4), called O4a and comprising data taken between 24 May 2023 and 16 January 2024. The GW signals targeted by this search are the so-called "long-duration" (> 1 s) transients expected from a variety of astrophysical processes, including non-axisymmetric deformations in magnetars or eccentric binary coalescences. We make minimal assumptions on the emitted GW waveforms in terms of morphologies and durations. Overall, our search targets signals with durations ~1-1000 s and frequency content in the range 16-2048 Hz. In the absence of significant detections, we report the sensitivity limits of our search in terms of root-sum-square signal amplitude (hrss) of reference waveforms. These limits improve upon the results from the third LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observing run (O3) by about 30% on average. Moreover, this analysis demonstrates substantial progress in our ability to search for long-duration GW signals owing to enhancements in pipeline detection efficiencies. As detector sensitivities continue to advance and observational runs grow longer, unmodeled long-duration searches will increasingly be able to explore a range of compelling astrophysical scenarios involving neutron stars and black holes.

evidence.title: Observation of the rare $B^0_s\toμ^+μ^-$ decay from the combined analysis of CMS and LHCb data
evidence.text: A joint measurement is presented of the branching fractions $B^0_s\toμ^+μ^-$ and $B^0\toμ^+μ^-$ in proton-proton collisions at the LHC by the CMS and LHCb experiments. The data samples were collected in 2011 at a centre-of-mass energy of 7 TeV, and in 2012 at 8 TeV. The combined analysis produces the first observation of the $B^0_s\toμ^+μ^-$ decay, with a statistical significance exceeding six standard deviations, and the best measurement of its branching fraction so far. Furthermore, evidence for the $B^0\toμ^+μ^-$ decay is obtained with a statistical significance of three standard deviations. The branching fraction measurements are statistically compatible with SM predictions and impose stringent constraints on several theories beyond the SM.

evidence.title: All-sky Searches for Continuous Gravitational Waves from Isolated Neutron Stars in the Data from the First Part of the Fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Observing Run
evidence.text: We present results from an all-sky search for continuous gravitational waves, using three different methods applied to the first eight months of LIGO data from the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration s observing run. We aim at signals potentially emitted by rotating, non-axisymmetric isolated neutron star in the Milky Way. The analysis spans a frequency range from 20 Hz to 2000 Hz and accommodates frequency derivative magnitudes up to $10^{-8}$ Hz/s. No statistically significant periodic gravitational wave signals were detected. We establish 95% confidence-level (CL) frequentist upper limits on the dimensionless strain amplitudes. The most stringent population-averaged strain upper limits reach 9.7 $\times$ $10^{-26}$ near 290 Hz, matching the best previous constraints from 250 to $\sim$1700 Hz while extending coverage to a much broader spin-down range. At higher frequencies, the new limits improve upon previous results by factors of approximately $\sim$1.6. These constraints are applied to three astrophysical scenarios: 1) the distribution of galactic neutron stars as a function of spin frequency and ellipticity; 2) the contribution of millisecond pulsars to the GeV excess near the galactic center; and 3) the possible dark matter fraction composed of nearby inspiraling primordial binary black holes with asteroid-scale masses.

prompt.user: {"mode": "web", "user_request": "Assess this candidate against prior work and technical evidence. Determine whether its specific mechanism has already been proposed and whether it is technically plausible. Read relevant sources; do not judge from result titles. Candidate: Kuramoto-Coupled Learning Rates: Phase-Locking G and D as Coupled Oscillators Treat the generator's and discriminator's loss trajectories as two coupled phase oscillators and import the Kuramoto synchronization model (statistical physics, 1975) to derive an explicit coupling-strength condition that keeps their update rates phase-locked, replacing the \"train D k times per G step\" folklore with a measurable synchronization index and a closed-form locking threshold. Strip away 'generator' and 'discriminator' and what remains is: two non-autonomous processes, each producing a roughly oscillatory scalar signal (the adversarial loss), coupled through a shared parameter (the minimax objective), where one process can outrun the other's ability to track it. This is exactly the structure that gave rise to the study of coupled oscillator synchronization: two (or many) periodic processes with different natural frequencies, weakly coupled, that either lock into a common phase or drift apart depending on coupling strength relative to their frequency mismatch. Kuramoto model (Yoshiki Kuramoto, 1975), developed to explain when populations of coupled oscillators (originally chemical/biological rhythms, later applied to power grids, neurons, fireflies) spontaneously phase-lock. Core object: each oscillator i has phase θ_i(t) evolving as dθ_i/dt = ω_i + (K/N) Σ_j sin(θ_j - θ_i). Core result: for two oscillators, phase-locking occurs iff coupling strength K exceeds the frequency mismatch |ω_1 - ω_2|; for large populations, a mean-field order parameter r = |⟨e^{iθ}⟩| measures the degree of synchronization, with a sharp critical coupling K_c above which r jumps from ~0 to a nontrivial locked value. - Oscillator phase θ_G(t), θ_D(t) ↔ instantaneous phase of the detrended G-loss and D-loss time series, extracted via Hilbert transform over a sliding training-step window. - Natural frequency ω_G, ω_D ↔ each network's current effective update rate (learning rate × recent gradient-driven loss oscillation frequency). - Coupling strength K ↔ a scalar hyperparameter that couples the two learning-rate schedules to each other, not to the data. - Order parameter r(t) = |(e^{iθ_G}+e^{iθ_D})/2| ↔ a literal, computable 'synchronization index' — the first direct instrumentation of the word 'synchronized' used in the original limitation. - Locking condition K > |ω_G - ω_D| ↔ a closed-form, checkable criterion for whether the current learning-rate ratio between G and D admits a phase-locked (stable, non-collapsing) regime at all. 1) During training, log G-loss and D-loss per step; detrend with a moving average and extract instantaneous phase via Hilbert transform in a rolling window of W steps. 2) Compute r(t) every W steps as the synchronization index. 3) Implement Kuramoto coupling as a multiplicative learning-rate correction: η_G(t) = η_G^0 · (1 + λ·K·sin(θ_D-θ_G)), η_D(t) = η_D^0 · (1 - λ·K·sin(θ_D-θ_G)), pulling the faster process's effective step size down and the slower one's up. 4) Online-adapt K itself via a simple controller (increase K when r(t) < r_min, e.g. 0.8, over a sustained window; decay K otherwise) to keep the pair inside the locked regime without hand-tuning a fixed k:1 D:G update ratio. 5) Log r(t) alongside FID/Inception Score-based mode-coverage metrics to test whether drops in r precede mode collapse. - Fixed-ratio heuristic: train D k times per G step (the original DCGAN/vanilla-GAN convention). - Two-Time-Scale Update Rule (separate fixed learning rates for G and D) — unverified, attributed to later literature (Heusel et al.), included as a non-coupled adaptive-rate baseline for contrast. - Unrolled GAN-style lookahead (Metz et al.) — unverified, included as a baseline that addresses the same instability via a different mechanism (unrolling D's future updates rather than phase-coupling). Kuramoto's guarantees hold for autonomous oscillators with fixed natural frequencies drawn from a stationary distribution, in the large-N mean-field limit, producing genuinely periodic signals. None of this holds cleanly for GAN training: the 'frequency' of loss oscillation is itself a nonstationary function of the evolving loss landscape (not fixed ω_i); there are only two 'oscillators,' so the mean-field order parameter degenerates to a raw two-point phase difference and loses its statistical meaning; and adversarial loss curves are frequently non-periodic, chaotic, or dominated by trend rather than oscillation, in which case the Hilbert-transform phase is not well-defined and the whole construction is meaningless noise. The transfer is therefore only as good as the empirical premise that GAN losses are quasi-periodic enough for phase extraction — this must be checked before anything else in the technique section is worth building. - Do G/D loss curves actually exhibit narrowband, Hilbert-transformable oscillation across common architectures (DCGAN, WGAN, StyleGAN-era), or is this only true in small toy settings? - Does the order parameter r(t) empirically anti-correlate with measured mode collapse (e.g., recall/coverage metrics or mode count on synthetic mixture-of-Gaussians data) before adding any correction — i.e., is r a useful *diagnostic* even if the coupling correction is never applied? - Is a two-oscillator Kuramoto coupling meaningfully different from just measuring the ratio of G and D loss magnitudes (a much simpler heuristic already implicit in some training tricks), or does the phase formalism add anything beyond restating existing signal in fancier language? - What window length W trades off phase-estimation stability against reaction lag, and does a lag long enough for a valid phase estimate arrive too late to prevent collapse? - Does the multiplicative learning-rate coupling interact badly with existing stabilizers (spectral normalization, gradient penalty), e.g., by fighting an already-adaptive optimizer like Adam? As the Transferer, the move here is to take the paper's own word — 'synchronized' — literally rather than as a metaphor, and ask what field actually solved the general problem of when two coupled periodic processes lock phase versus drift apart. That field is nonlinear dynamics / statistical physics, and the Kuramoto model is the canonical, decades-old answer, complete with a sharp analytic criterion (K vs. frequency mismatch) that the GAN literature's fixed-ratio heuristics lack entirely. The value of the transfer, if it holds, is not a new trick but a *measurement*: an explicit, checkable synchronization index (r) and a locking condition, replacing 'train D k times per G step, tuned by trial and error' with a quantity that can be logged and controlled. The central unverified premise — that GAN loss curves are oscillatory enough to have a meaningful instantaneous phase — is exactly where I would insist the idea be tested first, before any correction mechanism is trusted; if that premise fails, the whole transfer collapses and should be discarded rather than patched. TTUR and unrolled GANs are mentioned as prior mechanisms attacking the same limitation from the literature, not verified against this context, and are named to show where this proposal differs (a coupling law with a derivable threshold, rather than a fixed rate ratio or a truncated lookahead). Original task and gap: The gap: in the original GAN formulation, the discriminator must stay synchronized with the generator during training, since training G too much without updating D risks the 'Helvetica scenario' where many z values collapse to the same x, losing diversity (mode collapse). Generate 3 concrete research ideas that address this synchronization problem directly -- e.g. mechanisms to detect or prevent D/G training imbalance, adaptive update schedules, or alternative training dynamics that make the two networks robust to being out of sync. Ground each candidate in what is already known from the literature about GAN training instability and mode collapse. training G too much without updating D can cause the 'Helvetica scenario,' in which many z values collapse to the same x and the model loses diversity. - evidence (arxiv_1406.2661 / advantages_and_disadvantages): \"representation of $p_g(\\bm{x})$, and that $D$ must be synchronized well with $G$\" - verdict: partially_solved (confidence 0.6) ## Papers behind those gaps ### paper arxiv_1406.2661 (2014) **Generative Adversarial Networks** keywords: adversarial nets, generative model, discriminative model, minimax two-player game, multilayer perceptron, backpropagation, dropout, Jensen-Shannon divergence, Gaussian Parzen window problem: Estimating generative models that capture complex data distributions (e.g., natural images, audio, text) is difficult with existing maximum-likelihood-based approaches; the paper proposes instead to estimate generative models through an adversarial minimax game between a generator and a discriminator. motivation: Deep discriminative models have succeeded via backpropagation, dropout, and piecewise linear units, but deep generative models have had less impact because they require approximating intractable probabilistic computations and cannot easily leverage piecewise linear units in the generative context. prior limitations: - Maximum likelihood estimation and related strategies require approximating intractable probabilistic computations in deep generative models. - It is difficult to leverage piecewise linear units, which have well-behaved gradients, in the generative context. - Existing deep generative approaches rely on Markov chains or unrolled approximate inference networks during training and/or generation. approach: The authors define a minimax two-player game between a generative model G and a discriminative model D. G maps samples from a noise prior through a multilayer perceptron to synthesize data, while D estimates the probability that a sample came from the training data rather than from G. G is trained to maximize the probability of D making a mistake, and D is trained to minimize the same objective, using alternating backpropagation and dropout. In the space of arbitrary functions, the game has a unique equilibrium where G recovers the training data distribution and D equals 1/2 everywhere, with the criterion related to the Jensen-Shannon divergence between model and data distributions. Sampling from G requires only forward propagation, with no Markov chains or approximate inference. key ideas: - Minimax value function V(D,G) = E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 - D(G(z)))], optimized by alternating gradient updates. - Generator maps latent noise z from a prior through a multilayer perceptron into data space. - Discriminator is a classifier that estimates the probability that an input is real rather than generated. - In practice, G is trained to maximize log D(G(z)) instead of log(1 - D(G(z))) to avoid early saturation and provide stronger gradients. assumptions: - G and D are multilayer perceptrons (the special case called adversarial nets). - The theoretical equilibrium result holds in the space of arbitrary functions, i.e., with sufficient capacity. - For the convergence proof, D is allowed to reach its optimum given G before each generator update. - G and D are differentiable with respect to their parameters so the system can be trained by backpropagation. results: Adversarial nets can be trained with only backpropagation and dropout to generate plausible samples from MNIST, TFD, and CIFAR-10, and achieve Gaussian Parzen window log-likelihood estimates of 225 ± 2 on MNIST and 2057 ± 26 on TFD, surpassing the compared contemporary deep generative models. caveats: - The Gaussian Parzen window log-likelihood estimator has high variance and is acknowledged by the authors as an imperfect metric, especially in high-dimensional spaces. - Quantitative comparison covers only two datasets (MNIST and TFD); CIFAR-10 results are primarily qualitative. - The theoretical convergence guarantee assumes optimization in the space of arbitrary functions with sufficient capacity and optimal D updates, which is not satisfied by finite-capacity MLPs trained with gradient steps. - The non-saturating generator objective used in practice is a heuristic motivated by early gradient saturation. stated limitations: - There is no explicit representation of p_g(x); only samples can be drawn from the generator. - The discriminator must be synchronized with the generator during training; training G too much without updating D can cause the 'Helvetica scenario' in which many z values collapse to the same x. - The Gaussian Parzen window log-likelihood estimate has high variance and does not perform well in high-dimensional spaces, so the quantitative results are not definitive. open threads: - Conditional generative models p(x|c) can be obtained by adding c as input to both G and D. - Learned approximate inference can be performed by training an auxiliary network to predict z given x. - Approximately modeling all conditionals p(x_S | x_notS) via a family of shared-parameter conditional models. - Semi-supervised learning using features from the discriminator or an inference network when labeled data are limited. - Efficiency improvements through better coordination or division of the G and D training game. ## Also in the workspace (index only) _Not loaded — the rest of the workspace, by id. search_results.title: Measurement of the CKM angle $γ$ in $B^{\pm} \rightarrow D(\rightarrow K^{0}_{\rm S} h^{\prime+}h^{\prime-})h^{\pm}$ decays with a novel approach
search_results.snippet: A measurement of the CKM angle $γ$ and related strong-phase parameters is performed using a novel, model-independent approach in ${B^{\pm}\rightarrow D(\rightarrow K^{0}_{\rm S} h^{\prime+}h^{\prime-}) h^{\pm}}$ decays, where $h^{(\prime)} \equiv π, K$. The analysis uses a joint data sample of electron-positron collisions collected by the BESIII experiment at the Beijing Electron-Positron Collider II during 2010--2011 and 2021--2022, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 8 fb$^{-1}$, and proton-proton collisions collected by the LHCb experiment at the Large Hadron Collider during 2011--2018, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 9 fb$^{-1}$. The two datasets are analyzed simultaneously by applying per-event weights based on the amplitude variation over the $D$-decay phase space to enhance the sensitivity to $C\!P$-violating observables. The CKM angle $γ$ is determined to be $γ= (71.3\pm 5.0)^{\circ}$, which constitutes the most precise single measurement to date.

search_results.title: Search for High-energy Neutrinos from Binary Neutron Star Merger GW170817 with ANTARES, IceCube, and the Pierre Auger Observatory
search_results.snippet: The Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo observatories recently discovered gravitational waves from a binary neutron star inspiral. A short gamma-ray burst (GRB) that followed the merger of this binary was also recorded by the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (Fermi-GBM), and the Anticoincidence Shield for the Spectrometer for the International Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory (INTEGRAL), indicating particle acceleration by the source. The precise location of the event was determined by optical detections of emission following the merger. We searched for high-energy neutrinos from the merger in the GeV--EeV energy range using the ANTARES, IceCube, and Pierre Auger Observatories. No neutrinos directionally coincident with the source were detected within $\pm500$ s around the merger time. Additionally, no MeV neutrino burst signal was detected coincident with the merger. We further carried out an extended search in the direction of the source for high-energy neutrinos within the 14-day period following the merger, but found no evidence of emission. We used these results to probe dissipation mechanisms in relativistic outflows driven by the binary neutron star merger. The non-detection is consistent with model predictions of short GRBs observed at a large off-axis angle.

search_results.title: All-sky search for long-duration gravitational-wave transients in the first part of the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Observing run
search_results.snippet: We present an all-sky search for long-duration gravitational waves (GWs) from the first part of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA fourth observing run (O4), called O4a and comprising data taken between 24 May 2023 and 16 January 2024. The GW signals targeted by this search are the so-called "long-duration" (> 1 s) transients expected from a variety of astrophysical processes, including non-axisymmetric deformations in magnetars or eccentric binary coalescences. We make minimal assumptions on the emitted GW waveforms in terms of morphologies and durations. Overall, our search targets signals with durations ~1-1000 s and frequency content in the range 16-2048 Hz. In the absence of significant detections, we report the sensitivity limits of our search in terms of root-sum-square signal amplitude (hrss) of reference waveforms. These limits improve upon the results from the third LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observing run (O3) by about 30% on average. Moreover, this analysis demonstrates substantial progress in our ability to search for long-duration GW signals owing to enhancements in pipeline detection efficiencies. As detector sensitivities continue to advance and observational runs grow longer, unmodeled long-duration searches will increasingly be able to explore a range of compelling astrophysical scenarios involving neutron stars and black holes.

search_results.title: Observation of the rare $B^0_s\toμ^+μ^-$ decay from the combined analysis of CMS and LHCb data
search_results.snippet: A joint measurement is presented of the branching fractions $B^0_s\toμ^+μ^-$ and $B^0\toμ^+μ^-$ in proton-proton collisions at the LHC by the CMS and LHCb experiments. The data samples were collected in 2011 at a centre-of-mass energy of 7 TeV, and in 2012 at 8 TeV. The combined analysis produces the first observation of the $B^0_s\toμ^+μ^-$ decay, with a statistical significance exceeding six standard deviations, and the best measurement of its branching fraction so far. Furthermore, evidence for the $B^0\toμ^+μ^-$ decay is obtained with a statistical significance of three standard deviations. The branching fraction measurements are statistically compatible with SM predictions and impose stringent constraints on several theories beyond the SM.

search_results.title: All-sky Searches for Continuous Gravitational Waves from Isolated Neutron Stars in the Data from the First Part of the Fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Observing Run
search_results.snippet: We present results from an all-sky search for continuous gravitational waves, using three different methods applied to the first eight months of LIGO data from the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration s observing run. We aim at signals potentially emitted by rotating, non-axisymmetric isolated neutron star in the Milky Way. The analysis spans a frequency range from 20 Hz to 2000 Hz and accommodates frequency derivative magnitudes up to $10^{-8}$ Hz/s. No statistically significant periodic gravitational wave signals were detected. We establish 95% confidence-level (CL) frequentist upper limits on the dimensionless strain amplitudes. The most stringent population-averaged strain upper limits reach 9.7 $\times$ $10^{-26}$ near 290 Hz, matching the best previous constraints from 250 to $\sim$1700 Hz while extending coverage to a much broader spin-down range. At higher frequencies, the new limits improve upon previous results by factors of approximately $\sim$1.6. These constraints are applied to three astrophysical scenarios: 1) the distribution of galactic neutron stars as a function of spin frequency and ellipticity; 2) the contribution of millisecond pulsars to the GeV excess near the galactic center; and 3) the possible dark matter fraction composed of nearby inspiraling primordial binary black holes with asteroid-scale masses.

evidence.title: Measurement of the CKM angle $γ$ in $B^{\pm} \rightarrow D(\rightarrow K^{0}_{\rm S} h^{\prime+}h^{\prime-})h^{\pm}$ decays with a novel approach
evidence.text: A measurement of the CKM angle $γ$ and related strong-phase parameters is performed using a novel, model-independent approach in ${B^{\pm}\rightarrow D(\rightarrow K^{0}_{\rm S} h^{\prime+}h^{\prime-}) h^{\pm}}$ decays, where $h^{(\prime)} \equiv π, K$. The analysis uses a joint data sample of electron-positron collisions collected by the BESIII experiment at the Beijing Electron-Positron Collider II during 2010--2011 and 2021--2022, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 8 fb$^{-1}$, and proton-proton collisions collected by the LHCb experiment at the Large Hadron Collider during 2011--2018, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 9 fb$^{-1}$. The two datasets are analyzed simultaneously by applying per-event weights based on the amplitude variation over the $D$-decay phase space to enhance the sensitivity to $C\!P$-violating observables. The CKM angle $γ$ is determined to be $γ= (71.3\pm 5.0)^{\circ}$, which constitutes the most precise single measurement to date.

evidence.title: Search for High-energy Neutrinos from Binary Neutron Star Merger GW170817 with ANTARES, IceCube, and the Pierre Auger Observatory
evidence.text: The Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo observatories recently discovered gravitational waves from a binary neutron star inspiral. A short gamma-ray burst (GRB) that followed the merger of this binary was also recorded by the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (Fermi-GBM), and the Anticoincidence Shield for the Spectrometer for the International Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory (INTEGRAL), indicating particle acceleration by the source. The precise location of the event was determined by optical detections of emission following the merger. We searched for high-energy neutrinos from the merger in the GeV--EeV energy range using the ANTARES, IceCube, and Pierre Auger Observatories. No neutrinos directionally coincident with the source were detected within $\pm500$ s around the merger time. Additionally, no MeV neutrino burst signal was detected coincident with the merger. We further carried out an extended search in the direction of the source for high-energy neutrinos within the 14-day period following the merger, but found no evidence of emission. We used these results to probe dissipation mechanisms in relativistic outflows driven by the binary neutron star merger. The non-detection is consistent with model predictions of short GRBs observed at a large off-axis angle.

evidence.title: All-sky search for long-duration gravitational-wave transients in the first part of the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Observing run
evidence.text: We present an all-sky search for long-duration gravitational waves (GWs) from the first part of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA fourth observing run (O4), called O4a and comprising data taken between 24 May 2023 and 16 January 2024. The GW signals targeted by this search are the so-called "long-duration" (> 1 s) transients expected from a variety of astrophysical processes, including non-axisymmetric deformations in magnetars or eccentric binary coalescences. We make minimal assumptions on the emitted GW waveforms in terms of morphologies and durations. Overall, our search targets signals with durations ~1-1000 s and frequency content in the range 16-2048 Hz. In the absence of significant detections, we report the sensitivity limits of our search in terms of root-sum-square signal amplitude (hrss) of reference waveforms. These limits improve upon the results from the third LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observing run (O3) by about 30% on average. Moreover, this analysis demonstrates substantial progress in our ability to search for long-duration GW signals owing to enhancements in pipeline detection efficiencies. As detector sensitivities continue to advance and observational runs grow longer, unmodeled long-duration searches will increasingly be able to explore a range of compelling astrophysical scenarios involving neutron stars and black holes.

evidence.title: Observation of the rare $B^0_s\toμ^+μ^-$ decay from the combined analysis of CMS and LHCb data
evidence.text: A joint measurement is presented of the branching fractions $B^0_s\toμ^+μ^-$ and $B^0\toμ^+μ^-$ in proton-proton collisions at the LHC by the CMS and LHCb experiments. The data samples were collected in 2011 at a centre-of-mass energy of 7 TeV, and in 2012 at 8 TeV. The combined analysis produces the first observation of the $B^0_s\toμ^+μ^-$ decay, with a statistical significance exceeding six standard deviations, and the best measurement of its branching fraction so far. Furthermore, evidence for the $B^0\toμ^+μ^-$ decay is obtained with a statistical significance of three standard deviations. The branching fraction measurements are statistically compatible with SM predictions and impose stringent constraints on several theories beyond the SM.

evidence.title: All-sky Searches for Continuous Gravitational Waves from Isolated Neutron Stars in the Data from the First Part of the Fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Observing Run
evidence.text: We present results from an all-sky search for continuous gravitational waves, using three different methods applied to the first eight months of LIGO data from the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration s observing run. We aim at signals potentially emitted by rotating, non-axisymmetric isolated neutron star in the Milky Way. The analysis spans a frequency range from 20 Hz to 2000 Hz and accommodates frequency derivative magnitudes up to $10^{-8}$ Hz/s. No statistically significant periodic gravitational wave signals were detected. We establish 95% confidence-level (CL) frequentist upper limits on the dimensionless strain amplitudes. The most stringent population-averaged strain upper limits reach 9.7 $\times$ $10^{-26}$ near 290 Hz, matching the best previous constraints from 250 to $\sim$1700 Hz while extending coverage to a much broader spin-down range. At higher frequencies, the new limits improve upon previous results by factors of approximately $\sim$1.6. These constraints are applied to three astrophysical scenarios: 1) the distribution of galactic neutron stars as a function of spin frequency and ellipticity; 2) the contribution of millisecond pulsars to the GeV excess near the galactic center; and 3) the possible dark matter fraction composed of nearby inspiraling primordial binary black holes with asteroid-scale masses.

prompt.user: {"mode": "web", "user_request": "Assess this candidate against prior work and technical evidence. Determine whether its specific mechanism has already been proposed and whether it is technically plausible. Read relevant sources; do not judge from result titles. Candidate: Kuramoto-Coupled Learning Rates: Phase-Locking G and D as Coupled Oscillators Treat the generator's and discriminator's loss trajectories as two coupled phase oscillators and import the Kuramoto synchronization model (statistical physics, 1975) to derive an explicit coupling-strength condition that keeps their update rates phase-locked, replacing the \"train D k times per G step\" folklore with a measurable synchronization index and a closed-form locking threshold. Strip away 'generator' and 'discriminator' and what remains is: two non-autonomous processes, each producing a roughly oscillatory scalar signal (the adversarial loss), coupled through a shared parameter (the minimax objective), where one process can outrun the other's ability to track it. This is exactly the structure that gave rise to the study of coupled oscillator synchronization: two (or many) periodic processes with different natural frequencies, weakly coupled, that either lock into a common phase or drift apart depending on coupling strength relative to their frequency mismatch. Kuramoto model (Yoshiki Kuramoto, 1975), developed to explain when populations of coupled oscillators (originally chemical/biological rhythms, later applied to power grids, neurons, fireflies) spontaneously phase-lock. Core object: each oscillator i has phase θ_i(t) evolving as dθ_i/dt = ω_i + (K/N) Σ_j sin(θ_j - θ_i). Core result: for two oscillators, phase-locking occurs iff coupling strength K exceeds the frequency mismatch |ω_1 - ω_2|; for large populations, a mean-field order parameter r = |⟨e^{iθ}⟩| measures the degree of synchronization, with a sharp critical coupling K_c above which r jumps from ~0 to a nontrivial locked value. - Oscillator phase θ_G(t), θ_D(t) ↔ instantaneous phase of the detrended G-loss and D-loss time series, extracted via Hilbert transform over a sliding training-step window. - Natural frequency ω_G, ω_D ↔ each network's current effective update rate (learning rate × recent gradient-driven loss oscillation frequency). - Coupling strength K ↔ a scalar hyperparameter that couples the two learning-rate schedules to each other, not to the data. - Order parameter r(t) = |(e^{iθ_G}+e^{iθ_D})/2| ↔ a literal, computable 'synchronization index' — the first direct instrumentation of the word 'synchronized' used in the original limitation. - Locking condition K > |ω_G - ω_D| ↔ a closed-form, checkable criterion for whether the current learning-rate ratio between G and D admits a phase-locked (stable, non-collapsing) regime at all. 1) During training, log G-loss and D-loss per step; detrend with a moving average and extract instantaneous phase via Hilbert transform in a rolling window of W steps. 2) Compute r(t) every W steps as the synchronization index. 3) Implement Kuramoto coupling as a multiplicative learning-rate correction: η_G(t) = η_G^0 · (1 + λ·K·sin(θ_D-θ_G)), η_D(t) = η_D^0 · (1 - λ·K·sin(θ_D-θ_G)), pulling the faster process's effective step size down and the slower one's up. 4) Online-adapt K itself via a simple controller (increase K when r(t) < r_min, e.g. 0.8, over a sustained window; decay K otherwise) to keep the pair inside the locked regime without hand-tuning a fixed k:1 D:G update ratio. 5) Log r(t) alongside FID/Inception Score-based mode-coverage metrics to test whether drops in r precede mode collapse. - Fixed-ratio heuristic: train D k times per G step (the original DCGAN/vanilla-GAN convention). - Two-Time-Scale Update Rule (separate fixed learning rates for G and D) — unverified, attributed to later literature (Heusel et al.), included as a non-coupled adaptive-rate baseline for contrast. - Unrolled GAN-style lookahead (Metz et al.) — unverified, included as a baseline that addresses the same instability via a different mechanism (unrolling D's future updates rather than phase-coupling). Kuramoto's guarantees hold for autonomous oscillators with fixed natural frequencies drawn from a stationary distribution, in the large-N mean-field limit, producing genuinely periodic signals. None of this holds cleanly for GAN training: the 'frequency' of loss oscillation is itself a nonstationary function of the evolving loss landscape (not fixed ω_i); there are only two 'oscillators,' so the mean-field order parameter degenerates to a raw two-point phase difference and loses its statistical meaning; and adversarial loss curves are frequently non-periodic, chaotic, or dominated by trend rather than oscillation, in which case the Hilbert-transform phase is not well-defined and the whole construction is meaningless noise. The transfer is therefore only as good as the empirical premise that GAN losses are quasi-periodic enough for phase extraction — this must be checked before anything else in the technique section is worth building. - Do G/D loss curves actually exhibit narrowband, Hilbert-transformable oscillation across common architectures (DCGAN, WGAN, StyleGAN-era), or is this only true in small toy settings? - Does the order parameter r(t) empirically anti-correlate with measured mode collapse (e.g., recall/coverage metrics or mode count on synthetic mixture-of-Gaussians data) before adding any correction — i.e., is r a useful *diagnostic* even if the coupling correction is never applied? - Is a two-oscillator Kuramoto coupling meaningfully different from just measuring the ratio of G and D loss magnitudes (a much simpler heuristic already implicit in some training tricks), or does the phase formalism add anything beyond restating existing signal in fancier language? - What window length W trades off phase-estimation stability against reaction lag, and does a lag long enough for a valid phase estimate arrive too late to prevent collapse? - Does the multiplicative learning-rate coupling interact badly with existing stabilizers (spectral normalization, gradient penalty), e.g., by fighting an already-adaptive optimizer like Adam? As the Transferer, the move here is to take the paper's own word — 'synchronized' — literally rather than as a metaphor, and ask what field actually solved the general problem of when two coupled periodic processes lock phase versus drift apart. That field is nonlinear dynamics / statistical physics, and the Kuramoto model is the canonical, decades-old answer, complete with a sharp analytic criterion (K vs. frequency mismatch) that the GAN literature's fixed-ratio heuristics lack entirely. The value of the transfer, if it holds, is not a new trick but a *measurement*: an explicit, checkable synchronization index (r) and a locking condition, replacing 'train D k times per G step, tuned by trial and error' with a quantity that can be logged and controlled. The central unverified premise — that GAN loss curves are oscillatory enough to have a meaningful instantaneous phase — is exactly where I would insist the idea be tested first, before any correction mechanism is trusted; if that premise fails, the whole transfer collapses and should be discarded rather than patched. TTUR and unrolled GANs are mentioned as prior mechanisms attacking the same limitation from the literature, not verified against this context, and are named to show where this proposal differs (a coupling law with a derivable threshold, rather than a fixed rate ratio or a truncated lookahead). Original task and gap: The gap: in the original GAN formulation, the discriminator must stay synchronized with the generator during training, since training G too much without updating D risks the 'Helvetica scenario' where many z values collapse to the same x, losing diversity (mode collapse). Generate 3 concrete research ideas that address this synchronization problem directly -- e.g. mechanisms to detect or prevent D/G training imbalance, adaptive update schedules, or alternative training dynamics that make the two networks robust to being out of sync. Ground each candidate in what is already known from the literature about GAN training instability and mode collapse. Candidate:
Decoupling Diversity from D: A Synchronization-Free Anti-Collapse Channel
Give the generator a second, discriminator-independent signal against mode collapse — a latent-recovery constraint — so that anti-collapse pressure survives even when D has fallen out of sync with G.
The load-bearing assumption in the 1406.2661 formulation is that diversity in p_g is discovered and enforced *exclusively through the adversarial channel* — D's local curvature/calibration is the only carrier of information about whether distinct z values are producing distinct x. The convergence proof even assumes D reaches its optimum before each G step (gap_7d5bc91f); in practice this is approximated by a fixed D:G step ratio. The 'Helvetica scenario' is a direct symptom of this single-channel design: if the one channel goes stale, the safeguard vanishes entirely. This has been validated only in the regime where D actually is kept near-current (small MLPs on MNIST/TFD, with careful step ratios) — it has never been tested against what happens structurally if you refuse to keep D current.
- Add an encoder E_φ(x) → ẑ trained alongside G and D, with its own optimizer.
- Add a term to G's loss that does NOT route through D: an invertibility / latent-recovery penalty L_rec = E_z[ dist(E_φ(G(z)), z) ], using a noise-contrastive formulation (distinguish true (z, G(z)) pairs from shuffled/mismatched pairs, à la InfoGAN's MI lower bound or BiGAN-style joint encoding) rather than raw L2 regression, to avoid trivial degenerate solutions where E ignores x.
- G's total loss becomes: adversarial term (from whatever D currently is, however stale) + λ · L_rec. The adversarial term still pushes realism; L_rec independently pushes injectivity of the z→x map, which is precisely what collapses when many z map to one x.
- Optionally, monitor a 'sync-gap' statistic (e.g., D's real/fake loss variance over a sliding window, or how many G-steps have elapsed since D's last update) and use it to modulate λ upward specifically during detected desynchronization — but the core claim to test is that even a *constant* λ already buys robustness, because the mechanism doesn't depend on knowing D's state at all.
- Stress test: deliberately desynchronize training (freeze D for K steps, or run G:D at 10:1, 50:1) on toy mixture-of-Gaussians / stacked-MNIST setups used in prior mode-collapse studies, and measure mode coverage / reverse-KL to the true mixture as a function of desync severity, comparing vanilla GAN vs GAN+E across severities.
This is not the standard 'fix the schedule' move (adaptive D:G step ratios, D accuracy thresholds) which keeps the single-channel design intact and just tries to service it better. It is not full unrolled-GAN foresight either, which gives G information about D's *future* optimum but still routes all diversity pressure through D. Here the anti-collapse signal is architecturally independent of D's currency — the research question shifts from 'how do we keep D synchronized' to 'how much of the anti-collapse burden can be moved off the adversarial channel entirely, and what does the resulting realism/diversity trade-off look like as a function of sync quality.'
- Does the encoder itself introduce a *new* sync problem (E must stay reasonably current with G, just possibly on a more forgiving schedule) — i.e., have we relocated the fragility rather than removed it?
- Is there a degenerate regime where G satisfies L_rec by producing highly distinct-but-unrealistic x per z, trading mode coverage for sample quality — and how does λ trade against that?
- Under severe D desynchronization, does the adversarial term become actively harmful (pushing toward realism gains that undo L_rec's diversity gains), and is there an interaction effect worth measuring rather than the two terms just adding linearly?
- Is the benefit actually coming from injectivity enforcement, or just from adding *any* second gradient source that dilutes overfitting to a stale D — an ablation with a non-invertibility auxiliary loss (e.g. plain batch-diversity penalty) is needed to isolate the mechanism.
Stance: rather than proposing a better watchdog for D/G balance (which accepts that diversity must flow through D and tries to keep the pipe open), I am naming that single-channel design as the actual assumption at fault and inverting it — building a diversity channel that is structurally decoupled from D's currency. This borrows components from InfoGAN and BiGAN/ALI (unverified: exact citations and their original motivations were representation learning / mutual information maximization, not sync-robustness), but repurposes them explicitly as an anti-collapse mechanism to be stress-tested under deliberate desynchronization, which is a different framing and a different experiment than either paper ran. The claim that this improves robustness under desync is untested and is the thing this idea proposes to establish.

## Papers behind those gaps
### paper arxiv_1406.2661 (2014)
**Generative Adversarial Networks**
keywords: adversarial nets, generative model, discriminative model, minimax two-player game, multilayer perceptron, backpropagation, dropout, Jensen-Shannon divergence, Gaussian Parzen window
problem: Estimating generative models that capture complex data distributions (e.g., natural images, audio, text) is difficult with existing maximum-likelihood-based approaches; the paper proposes instead to estimate generative models through an adversarial minimax game between a generator and a discriminator.
motivation: Deep discriminative models have succeeded via backpropagation, dropout, and piecewise linear units, but deep generative models have had less impact because they require approximating intractable probabilistic computations and cannot easily leverage piecewise linear units in the generative context.
  prior limitations:
    - Maximum likelihood estimation and related strategies require approximating intractable probabilistic computations in deep generative models.
    - It is difficult to leverage piecewise linear units, which have well-behaved gradients, in the generative context.
    - Existing deep generative approaches rely on Markov chains or unrolled approximate inference networks during training and/or generation.
approach: The authors define a minimax two-player game between a generative model G and a discriminative model D. G maps samples from a noise prior through a multilayer perceptron to synthesize data, while D estimates the probability that a sample came from the training data rather than from G. G is trained to maximize the probability of D making a mistake, and D is trained to minimize the same objective, using alternating backpropagation and dropout. In the space of arbitrary functions, the game has a unique equilibrium where G recovers the training data distribution and D equals 1/2 everywhere, with the criterion related to the Jensen-Shannon divergence between model and data distributions. Sampling from G requires only forward propagation, with no Markov chains or approximate inference.
  key ideas:
    - Minimax value function V(D,G) = E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 - D(G(z)))], optimized by alternating gradient updates.
    - Generator maps latent noise z from a prior through a multilayer perceptron into data space.
    - Discriminator is a classifier that estimates the probability that an input is real rather than generated.
    - In practice, G is trained to maximize log D(G(z)) instead of log(1 - D(G(z))) to avoid early saturation and provide stronger gradients.
  assumptions:
    - G and D are multilayer perceptrons (the special case called adversarial nets).
    - The theoretical equilibrium result holds in the space of arbitrary functions, i.e., with sufficient capacity.
    - For the convergence proof, D is allowed to reach its optimum given G before each generator update.
    - G and D are differentiable with respect to their parameters so the system can be trained by backpropagation.
results: Adversarial nets can be trained with only backpropagation and dropout to generate plausible samples from MNIST, TFD, and CIFAR-10, and achieve Gaussian Parzen window log-likelihood estimates of 225 ± 2 on MNIST and 2057 ± 26 on TFD, surpassing the compared contemporary deep generative models.
  caveats:
    - The Gaussian Parzen window log-likelihood estimator has high variance and is acknowledged by the authors as an imperfect metric, especially in high-dimensional spaces.
    - Quantitative comparison covers only two datasets (MNIST and TFD); CIFAR-10 results are primarily qualitative.
    - The theoretical convergence guarantee assumes optimization in the space of arbitrary functions with sufficient capacity and optimal D updates, which is not satisfied by finite-capacity MLPs trained with gradient steps.
    - The non-saturating generator objective used in practice is a heuristic motivated by early gradient saturation.
  stated limitations:
    - There is no explicit representation of p_g(x); only samples can be drawn from the generator.
    - The discriminator must be synchronized with the generator during training; training G too much without updating D can cause the 'Helvetica scenario' in which many z values collapse to the same x.
    - The Gaussian Parzen window log-likelihood estimate has high variance and does not perform well in high-dimensional spaces, so the quantitative results are not definitive.
  open threads:
    - Conditional generative models p(x|c) can be obtained by adding c as input to both G and D.
    - Learned approximate inference can be performed by training an auxiliary network to predict z given x.
    - Approximately modeling all conditionals p(x_S | x_notS) via a family of shared-parameter conditional models.
    - Semi-supervised learning using features from the discriminator or an inference network when labeled data are limited.
    - Efficiency improvements through better coordination or division of the G and D training game.

search_results.title: Test of lepton flavour universality using $B^0 \to D^{*-}τ^+ν_τ$ decays with hadronic $τ$ channels
search_results.snippet: The branching fraction $\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to D^{*-}τ^+ν_τ)$ is measured relative to that of the normalization mode $B^0 \to D^{*-}π^+π^-π^+$ using hadronic $τ^+ \to π^+π^-π^+(π^0)\overlineν_τ$ decays in proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV collected by the LHCb experiment, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 2 fb$^{-1}$. The measured ratio is $\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to D^{*-}τ^+ν_τ)/\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to D^{*-}π^+π^-π^+) = 1.79 \pm 0.11 \pm 0.11$, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second is related to systematic effects. Using established branching fractions for the $B^0 \to D^{*-}π^+π^-π^+$ and $B^0 \to D^{*-}μ^+ν_μ$ modes, the lepton universality test, $\mathcal{R}(D^{*-}) \equiv \mathcal{B}(B^0 \to D^{*-}τ^+ν_τ)/\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to D^{*-}μ^+ν_μ)$ is calculated, $$ \mathcal{R}(D^{*-}) = 0.260 \pm 0.015 \pm 0.016 \pm 0.012\, , $$ where the third uncertainty is due to the uncertainties on the external branching fractions. This result is consistent with the Standard Model prediction and with previous measurements.

search_results.title: Measurement of the CKM angle $γ$ in $B^{\pm} \rightarrow D(\rightarrow K^{0}_{\rm S} h^{\prime+}h^{\prime-})h^{\pm}$ decays with a novel approach
search_results.snippet: A measurement of the CKM angle $γ$ and related strong-phase parameters is performed using a novel, model-independent approach in ${B^{\pm}\rightarrow D(\rightarrow K^{0}_{\rm S} h^{\prime+}h^{\prime-}) h^{\pm}}$ decays, where $h^{(\prime)} \equiv π, K$. The analysis uses a joint data sample of electron-positron collisions collected by the BESIII experiment at the Beijing Electron-Positron Collider II during 2010--2011 and 2021--2022, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 8 fb$^{-1}$, and proton-proton collisions collected by the LHCb experiment at the Large Hadron Collider during 2011--2018, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 9 fb$^{-1}$. The two datasets are analyzed simultaneously by applying per-event weights based on the amplitude variation over the $D$-decay phase space to enhance the sensitivity to $C\!P$-violating observables. The CKM angle $γ$ is determined to be $γ= (71.3\pm 5.0)^{\circ}$, which constitutes the most precise single measurement to date.

search_results.title: Determination of quantum numbers for several excited charmed mesons observed in $B^- \to D^{*+} π^- π^-$ decays
search_results.snippet: A four-body amplitude analysis of the $B^- \to D^{*+} π^- π^-$ decay is performed, where fractions and relative phases of the various resonances contributing to the decay are measured. Several quasi-model-independent analyses are performed aimed at searching for the presence of new states and establishing the quantum numbers of previously observed charmed meson resonances. In particular the resonance parameters and quantum numbers are determined for the $D_1(2420)$, $D_1(2430)$, $D_0(2550)$, $D^*_1(2600)$, $D_2(2740)$ and $D^*_3(2750)$ states. The mixing between the $D_1(2420)$ and $D_1(2430)$ resonances is studied and the mixing parameters are measured. The dataset corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 4.7 $fb^{-1}$, collected in proton-proton collisions at center-of-mass energies of 7, 8 and 13 TeV with the LHCb detector.

search_results.title: Search for lepton-number-violating $B^-\to D^{(*)+}μ^-μ^-$ decays
search_results.snippet: A search is performed for lepton-number-violating $B^-\to D^{(*)+}μ^-μ^-$ decays, using data collected by the LHCb experiment in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 5.4 fb$^{-1}$. No significant signal is observed, and upper limits are set on the branching fractions, ${\cal B}(B^-\to D^{+}μ^-μ^-) < 4.6 \times 10^{-8}$ and ${\cal B}(B^-\to D^{*+}μ^-μ^-) < 5.9 \times 10^{-8}$, at the 95% confidence level.

search_results.title: Measurement of the $D^{*}$ longitudinal polarization in $B^0\to D^{*-}τ^{+}ν_τ$ decays
search_results.snippet: The longitudinal polarization fraction of the $D^{*}$ meson is measured in $B^0\to D^{*-}τ^{+}ν_τ$ decays, where the $τ$ lepton decays to three charged pions and a neutrino, using proton-proton collision data collected by the LHCb experiment at center-of-mass energies of 7, 8 and 13 TeV and corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 5 fb$^{-1}$. The $D^{*}$ polarization fraction $F_{L}^{D^{*}}$ is measured in two $q^{2}$ regions, below and above 7 GeV$^{2}/c^{4}$, where $q^{2}$ is defined as the squared invariant mass of the $τν_τ$ system. The $F_{L}^{D^{*}}$ values are measured to be $0.52 \pm 0.07 \pm 0.04$ and $0.34 \pm 0.08 \pm 0.02$ for the lower and higher $q^{2}$ regions, respectively. The first uncertainties are statistical and the second systematic. The average value over the whole $q^{2}$ range is: $$F_{L}^{D^{*}} = 0.41 \pm 0.06 \pm 0.03.$$ These results are compatible with the Standard Model predictions.

prompt.user: {"mode": "web", "user_request": "Assess this candidate against prior work and technical evidence. Determine whether its specific mechanism has already been proposed and whether it is technically plausible. Read relevant sources; do not judge from result titles. Candidate: Decoupling Diversity from D: A Synchronization-Free Anti-Collapse Channel Give the generator a second, discriminator-independent signal against mode collapse — a latent-recovery constraint — so that anti-collapse pressure survives even when D has fallen out of sync with G. The load-bearing assumption in the 1406.2661 formulation is that diversity in p_g is discovered and enforced *exclusively through the adversarial channel* — D's local curvature/calibration is the only carrier of information about whether distinct z values are producing distinct x. The convergence proof even assumes D reaches its optimum before each G step (gap_7d5bc91f); in practice this is approximated by a fixed D:G step ratio. The 'Helvetica scenario' is a direct symptom of this single-channel design: if the one channel goes stale, the safeguard vanishes entirely. This has been validated only in the regime where D actually is kept near-current (small MLPs on MNIST/TFD, with careful step ratios) — it has never been tested against what happens structurally if you refuse to keep D current. - Add an encoder E_φ(x) → ẑ trained alongside G and D, with its own optimizer. - Add a term to G's loss that does NOT route through D: an invertibility / latent-recovery penalty L_rec = E_z[ dist(E_φ(G(z)), z) ], using a noise-contrastive formulation (distinguish true (z, G(z)) pairs from shuffled/mismatched pairs, à la InfoGAN's MI lower bound or BiGAN-style joint encoding) rather than raw L2 regression, to avoid trivial degenerate solutions where E ignores x. - G's total loss becomes: adversarial term (from whatever D currently is, however stale) + λ · L_rec. The adversarial term still pushes realism; L_rec independently pushes injectivity of the z→x map, which is precisely what collapses when many z map to one x. - Optionally, monitor a 'sync-gap' statistic (e.g., D's real/fake loss variance over a sliding window, or how many G-steps have elapsed since D's last update) and use it to modulate λ upward specifically during detected desynchronization — but the core claim to test is that even a *constant* λ already buys robustness, because the mechanism doesn't depend on knowing D's state at all. - Stress test: deliberately desynchronize training (freeze D for K steps, or run G:D at 10:1, 50:1) on toy mixture-of-Gaussians / stacked-MNIST setups used in prior mode-collapse studies, and measure mode coverage / reverse-KL to the true mixture as a function of desync severity, comparing vanilla GAN vs GAN+E across severities. This is not the standard 'fix the schedule' move (adaptive D:G step ratios, D accuracy thresholds) which keeps the single-channel design intact and just tries to service it better. It is not full unrolled-GAN foresight either, which gives G information about D's *future* optimum but still routes all diversity pressure through D. Here the anti-collapse signal is architecturally independent of D's currency — the research question shifts from 'how do we keep D synchronized' to 'how much of the anti-collapse burden can be moved off the adversarial channel entirely, and what does the resulting realism/diversity trade-off look like as a function of sync quality.' - Does the encoder itself introduce a *new* sync problem (E must stay reasonably current with G, just possibly on a more forgiving schedule) — i.e., have we relocated the fragility rather than removed it? - Is there a degenerate regime where G satisfies L_rec by producing highly distinct-but-unrealistic x per z, trading mode coverage for sample quality — and how does λ trade against that? - Under severe D desynchronization, does the adversarial term become actively harmful (pushing toward realism gains that undo L_rec's diversity gains), and is there an interaction effect worth measuring rather than the two terms just adding linearly? - Is the benefit actually coming from injectivity enforcement, or just from adding *any* second gradient source that dilutes overfitting to a stale D — an ablation with a non-invertibility auxiliary loss (e.g. plain batch-diversity penalty) is needed to isolate the mechanism. Stance: rather than proposing a better watchdog for D/G balance (which accepts that diversity must flow through D and tries to keep the pipe open), I am naming that single-channel design as the actual assumption at fault and inverting it — building a diversity channel that is structurally decoupled from D's currency. This borrows components from InfoGAN and BiGAN/ALI (unverified: exact citations and their original motivations were representation learning / mutual information maximization, not sync-robustness), but repurposes them explicitly as an anti-collapse mechanism to be stress-tested under deliberate desynchronization, which is a different framing and a different experiment than either paper ran. The claim that this improves robustness under desync is untested and is the thing this idea proposes to establish. Original task and gap: The gap: in the original GAN formulation, the discriminator must stay synchronized with the generator during training, since training G too much without updating D risks the 'Helvetica scenario' where many z values collapse to the same x, losing diversity (mode collapse). Generate 3 concrete research ideas that address this synchronization problem directly -- e.g. mechanisms to detect or prevent D/G training imbalance, adaptive update schedules, or alternative training dynamics that make the two networks robust to being out of sync. Ground each candidate in what is already known from the literature about GAN training instability and mode collapse. Already loaded project context, including selected papers: ## Gaps in scope ### gap gap_f19d02aa [limitation] ← the user is currently focused on this one **Discriminator must stay synchronized with generator** canonical: generator and discriminator must remain synchronized to avoid mode collapse The discriminator must be synchronized well with the generator during training; training G too much without updating D can cause the 'Helvetica scenario,' in which many z values collapse to the same x and the model loses diversity. - evidence (arxiv_1406.2661 / advantages_and_disadvantages): \"representation of $p_g(\\bm{x})$, and that $D$ must be synchronized well with $G$\" - verdict: partially_solved (confidence 0.6) ## Papers behind those gaps ### paper arxiv_1406.2661 (2014) **Generative Adversarial Networks** keywords: adversarial nets, generative model, discriminative model, minimax two-player game, multilayer perceptron, backpropagation, dropout, Jensen-Shannon divergence, Gaussian Parzen window problem: Estimating generative models that capture complex data distributions (e.g., natural images, audio, text) is difficult with existing maximum-likelihood-based approaches; the paper proposes instead to estimate generative models through an adversarial minimax game between a generator and a discriminator. motivation: Deep discriminative models have succeeded via backpropagation, dropout, and piecewise linear units, but deep generative models have had less impact because they require approximating intractable probabilistic computations and cannot easily leverage piecewise linear units in the generative context. prior limitations: - Maximum likelihood estimation and related strategies require approximating intractable probabilistic computations in deep generative models. - It is difficult to leverage piecewise linear units, which have well-behaved gradients, in the generative context. - Existing deep generative approaches rely on Markov chains or unrolled approximate inference networks during training and/or generation. approach: The authors define a minimax two-player game between a generative model G and a discriminative model D. G maps samples from a noise prior through a multilayer perceptron to synthesize data, while D estimates the probability that a sample came from the training data rather than from G. G is trained to maximize the probability of D making a mistake, and D is trained to minimize the same objective, using alternating backpropagation and dropout. In the space of arbitrary functions, the game has a unique equilibrium where G recovers the training data distribution and D equals 1/2 everywhere, with the criterion related to the Jensen-Shannon divergence between model and data distributions. Sampling from G requires only forward propagation, with no Markov chains or approximate inference. key ideas: - Minimax value function V(D,G) = E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 - D(G(z)))], optimized by alternating gradient updates. - Generator maps latent noise z from a prior through a multilayer perceptron into data space. - Discriminator is a classifier that estimates the probability that an input is real rather than generated. - In practice, G is trained to maximize log D(G(z)) instead of log(1 - D(G(z))) to avoid early saturation and provide stronger gradients. assumptions: - G and D are multilayer perceptrons (the special case called adversarial nets). - The theoretical equilibrium result holds in the space of arbitrary functions, i.e., with sufficient capacity. - For the convergence proof, D is allowed to reach its optimum given G before each generator update. - G and D are differentiable with respect to their parameters so the system can be trained by backpropagation. results: Adversarial nets can be trained with only backpropagation and dropout to generate plausible samples from MNIST, TFD, and CIFAR-10, and achieve Gaussian Parzen window log-likelihood estimates of 225 ± 2 on MNIST and 2057 ± 26 on TFD, surpassing the compared contemporary deep generative models. caveats: - The Gaussian Parzen window log-likelihood estimator has high variance and is acknowledged by the authors as an imperfect metric, especially in high-dimensional spaces. - Quantitative comparison covers only two datasets (MNIST and TFD); CIFAR-10 results are primarily qualitative. - The theoretical convergence guarantee assumes optimization in the space of arbitrary functions with sufficient capacity and optimal D updates, which is not satisfied by finite-capacity MLPs trained with gradient steps. - The non-saturating generator objective used in practice is a heuristic motivated by early gradient saturation. stated limitations: - There is no explicit representation of p_g(x); only samples can be drawn from the generator. - The discriminator must be synchronized with the generator during training; training G too much without updating D can cause the 'Helvetica scenario' in which many z values collapse to the same x. - The Gaussian Parzen window log-likelihood estimate has high variance and does not perform well in high-dimensional spaces, so the quantitative results are not definitive. open threads: - Conditional generative models p(x|c) can be obtained by adding c as input to both G and D. - Learned approximate inference can be performed by training an auxiliary network to predict z given x. - Approximately modeling all conditionals p(x_S | x_notS) via a family of shared-parameter conditional models. - Semi-supervised learning using features from the discriminator or an inference network when labeled data are limited. - Efficiency improvements through better coordination or division of the G and D training game. ## Also in the workspace (index only) _Not loaded — the rest of the workspace, by id. search_results.title: Test of lepton flavour universality using $B^0 \to D^{*-}τ^+ν_τ$ decays with hadronic $τ$ channels
search_results.snippet: The branching fraction $\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to D^{*-}τ^+ν_τ)$ is measured relative to that of the normalization mode $B^0 \to D^{*-}π^+π^-π^+$ using hadronic $τ^+ \to π^+π^-π^+(π^0)\overlineν_τ$ decays in proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV collected by the LHCb experiment, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 2 fb$^{-1}$. The measured ratio is $\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to D^{*-}τ^+ν_τ)/\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to D^{*-}π^+π^-π^+) = 1.79 \pm 0.11 \pm 0.11$, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second is related to systematic effects. Using established branching fractions for the $B^0 \to D^{*-}π^+π^-π^+$ and $B^0 \to D^{*-}μ^+ν_μ$ modes, the lepton universality test, $\mathcal{R}(D^{*-}) \equiv \mathcal{B}(B^0 \to D^{*-}τ^+ν_τ)/\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to D^{*-}μ^+ν_μ)$ is calculated, $$ \mathcal{R}(D^{*-}) = 0.260 \pm 0.015 \pm 0.016 \pm 0.012\, , $$ where the third uncertainty is due to the uncertainties on the external branching fractions. This result is consistent with the Standard Model prediction and with previous measurements.

search_results.title: Measurement of the CKM angle $γ$ in $B^{\pm} \rightarrow D(\rightarrow K^{0}_{\rm S} h^{\prime+}h^{\prime-})h^{\pm}$ decays with a novel approach
search_results.snippet: A measurement of the CKM angle $γ$ and related strong-phase parameters is performed using a novel, model-independent approach in ${B^{\pm}\rightarrow D(\rightarrow K^{0}_{\rm S} h^{\prime+}h^{\prime-}) h^{\pm}}$ decays, where $h^{(\prime)} \equiv π, K$. The analysis uses a joint data sample of electron-positron collisions collected by the BESIII experiment at the Beijing Electron-Positron Collider II during 2010--2011 and 2021--2022, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 8 fb$^{-1}$, and proton-proton collisions collected by the LHCb experiment at the Large Hadron Collider during 2011--2018, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 9 fb$^{-1}$. The two datasets are analyzed simultaneously by applying per-event weights based on the amplitude variation over the $D$-decay phase space to enhance the sensitivity to $C\!P$-violating observables. The CKM angle $γ$ is determined to be $γ= (71.3\pm 5.0)^{\circ}$, which constitutes the most precise single measurement to date.

search_results.title: Determination of quantum numbers for several excited charmed mesons observed in $B^- \to D^{*+} π^- π^-$ decays
search_results.snippet: A four-body amplitude analysis of the $B^- \to D^{*+} π^- π^-$ decay is performed, where fractions and relative phases of the various resonances contributing to the decay are measured. Several quasi-model-independent analyses are performed aimed at searching for the presence of new states and establishing the quantum numbers of previously observed charmed meson resonances. In particular the resonance parameters and quantum numbers are determined for the $D_1(2420)$, $D_1(2430)$, $D_0(2550)$, $D^*_1(2600)$, $D_2(2740)$ and $D^*_3(2750)$ states. The mixing between the $D_1(2420)$ and $D_1(2430)$ resonances is studied and the mixing parameters are measured. The dataset corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 4.7 $fb^{-1}$, collected in proton-proton collisions at center-of-mass energies of 7, 8 and 13 TeV with the LHCb detector.

search_results.title: Search for lepton-number-violating $B^-\to D^{(*)+}μ^-μ^-$ decays
search_results.snippet: A search is performed for lepton-number-violating $B^-\to D^{(*)+}μ^-μ^-$ decays, using data collected by the LHCb experiment in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 5.4 fb$^{-1}$. No significant signal is observed, and upper limits are set on the branching fractions, ${\cal B}(B^-\to D^{+}μ^-μ^-) < 4.6 \times 10^{-8}$ and ${\cal B}(B^-\to D^{*+}μ^-μ^-) < 5.9 \times 10^{-8}$, at the 95% confidence level.

search_results.title: Measurement of the $D^{*}$ longitudinal polarization in $B^0\to D^{*-}τ^{+}ν_τ$ decays
search_results.snippet: The longitudinal polarization fraction of the $D^{*}$ meson is measured in $B^0\to D^{*-}τ^{+}ν_τ$ decays, where the $τ$ lepton decays to three charged pions and a neutrino, using proton-proton collision data collected by the LHCb experiment at center-of-mass energies of 7, 8 and 13 TeV and corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 5 fb$^{-1}$. The $D^{*}$ polarization fraction $F_{L}^{D^{*}}$ is measured in two $q^{2}$ regions, below and above 7 GeV$^{2}/c^{4}$, where $q^{2}$ is defined as the squared invariant mass of the $τν_τ$ system. The $F_{L}^{D^{*}}$ values are measured to be $0.52 \pm 0.07 \pm 0.04$ and $0.34 \pm 0.08 \pm 0.02$ for the lower and higher $q^{2}$ regions, respectively. The first uncertainties are statistical and the second systematic. The average value over the whole $q^{2}$ range is: $$F_{L}^{D^{*}} = 0.41 \pm 0.06 \pm 0.03.$$ These results are compatible with the Standard Model predictions.
